analysis.one_liner: Lets banks with branches in multiple states merge them into a single interstate bank, with state opt-outs.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after introduction it was referred to a House Banking subcommittee and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have let a bank holding company that owns banks in several states combine them into one bank with branches across state lines, starting June 1, 1995 [S3]. It paired that opening with safeguards: states could opt out and block the combinations, out-of-state branches would have to follow the host state's consumer protection and fair lending laws, regulators would have to weigh each bank's Community Reinvestment Act record, and states would gain power to tax and examine the out-of-state branches [S3]. It was referred to the House Banking Committee and then to a subcommittee, where it stayed until the Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Large bank holding companies operating banks in several states would gain the most, because they could merge those separate banks into one institution with branches in many states instead of running them as separate legal entities [S3]. Communities would also get something: federal regulators would have to consider each bank's Community Reinvestment Act record before approving a combination, banks with interstate branches would receive state-by-state CRA evaluations, and states could impose bank shares taxes and examine the records of federally chartered banks for state tax purposes [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Authorizes a bank holding company with subsidiary banks in more than one state to combine them into a single resulting bank by merger or consolidation, beginning June 1, 1995.
Requires the federal banking agency to consider each bank's Community Reinvestment Act rating and state community reinvestment views before approving a combination.
Requires branches created by an interstate combination to follow the host state's laws on intrastate branching, consumer protection, fair lending, and community reinvestment.
Adds state-by-state Community Reinvestment Act evaluations for any regulated financial institution with branches in two or more states.
Lets state tax authorities review the books and records of federally chartered banks with offices in the state, and lets host states impose a proportionate bank shares tax on out-of-state banks.

analysis.who_pays: Community banks and smaller local banks would face new competition from out-of-state giants able to convert acquired banks into branches, and some bank employees and local bank managements could be affected by consolidations. Consumers could face reduced local competition where combinations concentrate branches under one owner, though any state could prohibit combinations to prevent that [S3].

drawbacks.text: Allowing bank holding companies to combine banks across state lines could concentrate banking ownership and reduce local competition in some markets, which is why the bill lets states opt out of interstate combinations and leaves antitrust law fully applicable to them [S3].

The bill's structure was complicated: states could prohibit or permit combinations under different time windows and conditions, and a state could require a completed combination to be converted back into separate banks, creating uncertainty for banks and regulators [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was a compromise: it opened the door to interstate banking, which large multistate banks wanted, but kept states in control through opt-outs, host-state law, CRA scrutiny, and new state tax and examination powers. Its main downside was the possibility of banking concentration in some markets, which the state opt-out and antitrust provisions were meant to blunt. On balance it was more carefully constructed than a simple deregulation bill, but its core benefit still flowed to large banking companies.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in September 1993, sent to the House Banking Committee, then passed down to a subcommittee, and nothing further happened before the Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Rep. Carolyn Maloney introduced the Interstate Bank Consolidation Act of 1993 on September 23, 1993, and it was referred to the House Committee on Banking, Finance and Urban Affairs.
Three House Democrats cosponsored the bill.

On October 18, 1993, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions Supervision, Regulation and Deposit Insurance, and no further action was taken before the 103rd Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, interstate banking rules stayed as they were, which suited banks and bank holding companies comfortable with the existing state-by-state structure; no consolidations were authorized by this bill, and no new state tax or examination powers took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Banks content with the status quo

against.name: House Committee on Banking, Finance and Urban Affairs
against.what_they_did: Received the bill in September 1993 and referred it to a subcommittee on October 18, 1993; never reported it out or brought it to a vote.

against.name: Henry Gonzalez
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Banking, Finance and Urban Affairs
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee that never scheduled the bill for consideration, leaving it in subcommittee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Only a Democratic sponsor and three Democratic cosponsors appear in the record, and no votes were ever taken, so no partisan pattern is visible.

industries.note: The bill would have let companies with banks in several states merge them into one bank with branches across state lines, cutting the cost of running separate banks in each state. Safeguards like host-state law and CRA state-by-state reviews tempered the gain, and states could still opt out.

Out-of-state banking companies could have converted acquired local banks into branches, bringing larger competitors into local markets. States could prohibit interstate combinations, which would have limited the threat in opting-out states.

The bill would have given host states power to impose bank shares taxes on out-of-state banks, examine federally chartered banks' records for state tax purposes, and coordinate examinations of out-of-state branches.
